title: Torsion detection in clique complexes is conditionally $QMA_1$-hard
abstract: Quantum algorithms for topological data analysis compute Betti numbers, the ranks of the homology groups of a simplicial complex, which can be read off from the kernel of a combinatorial Laplacian. Deciding whether a Betti number of a clique complex is nonzero is $QMA_1$-hard, and remains so under a spectral gap promise on vertex-weighted graphs. Integral homology, however, contains information inaccessible to the Laplacian spectrum. A new part that appears in integral homology is torsion: cycles that become boundaries only after being traversed several times, as in a projective plane or a Klein bottle. We ask how hard it is to detect torsion, and we answer with a simple reduction. We attach to an arbitrary clique complex a fixed $31$-vertex triangulation of the projective plane. The $k$th mod-$2$ Betti number of the input then reappears as $2$-torsion two degrees up, while all rational homology disappears and every combinatorial Laplacian acquires a constant spectral gap. We conclude that detecting torsion in clique complexes of unweighted graphs is $NP$-hard, even under a constant gap promise, and that it is $QMA_1$-hard if mod-$2$ clique homology is.
summary: This paper establishes the computational hardness of detecting torsion in the homology of clique complexes, a structure derived from graphs. By using a specific algebraic gadget, the authors reduce the problem to detecting 2-torsion in a complex whose Laplacian is guaranteed to have a spectral gap. This proves the problem is NP-hard and QMA_1-hard, highlighting the unique information captured by integral homology beyond what is accessible via spectral methods.
main_problem: The paper determines the computational hardness of detecting torsion in the integral homology of clique complexes, which captures topological information inaccessible to standard spectral methods.
main_result: Detecting torsion in clique complexes of unweighted graphs is shown to be NP-hard, and it is QMA_1-hard under certain conditions related to mod-2 clique homology.
method: The authors construct a reduction by joining the input complex with a fixed gadget (triangulation of the projective plane) to encode the problem into the detection of 2-torsion in the resulting complex's homology.
model_or_system: The model is the clique complex of a graph, analyzed using algebraic topology (homology theory) and spectral graph theory (Laplacian operators). The core mathematical tool is the join operation on simplicial complexes.
key_observables: Betti numbers ($ eta_k$), integral homology groups ($	ext{e}H_k$), and the presence/absence of 2-torsion in the homology groups.
important_parameters: The spectral gap constant ($c_Y$) imposed by the gadget, and the degree of the homology group ($k$).
main_assumptions: The QMA_1-hardness result is conditional on the 2-torsion-freeness of the 'NO' instances of the original clique homology problem.
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes the reduction: joining the input with the projective plane removes rational homology, gaps every Laplacian, and re-encodes the $k$-th mod-2 Betti number as 2-torsion in degree $k+2$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the hardness proof by first establishing the algebraic machinery (Künneth formula, spectral gap via the join operation) and then constructing a specific reduction from the known hard problem of clique homology to the gapped torsion detection problem.
why_interesting: While the topic is purely in algebraic topology and quantum complexity theory, the use of spectral properties (Laplacian, spectral gap) to characterize computational hardness is relevant to understanding the limits of quantum algorithms in analyzing complex physical structures.
